blocks.text: Many government maps described interpreted conditions rather than surveyed ownership. Geological units classified rock and structure; soil maps grouped land from field observations; forestry maps recorded resources and management areas. The line on each map answered a different question.

blocks.text: The 1964 Northland National Resources Survey brought relief, communications, geology, soils, current land use and land-use potential into coordinated map sets. The 1959 Descriptive Atlas of New Zealand brought climate, geology, soils, vegetation, population, land classification, manufacturing and communications into one publication. Both projects asked readers to compare geographic themes, although each theme still lived on its own map.

blocks.text: For a GIS user, these boundaries need different metadata. A soil unit records a field-based classification; a cadastral line carries survey and legal evidence; a census boundary serves statistical administration. GIS can store each as the same geometry type, but the coordinates alone cannot explain what the line means or how certain it is.
